q: Clinical phases of amniotic fluid embolism — Phase I : Phase II.
opts: Phase I: sudden hypoxia, hypotension and shock with little bleeding — Phase II: haemorrhage from disseminated intravascular coagulation
Phase I: heavy bleeding with an atonic uterus — Phase II: hypoxia from pulmonary vasospasm and right heart strain
Phase I: high fever with uterine tenderness — Phase II: septic shock with acute kidney injury
Phase I: severe hypertension and convulsions — Phase II: hepatic failure with profound hypoglycaemia
exp: Phase I is respiratory and cardiovascular collapse with little bleeding, and phase II is the haemorrhagic phase from consumptive coagulopathy.

opts: 1 in 250 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
1 in 1000 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
1 in 50 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
1 in 10 — a risk at or above this cut-off is called screen-positive
exp: The standard second-trimester cut-off is 1 in 250: a risk of 1 in 150 is screen-positive and 1 in 500 is screen-negative.

opts: Mento-anterior: vaginal delivery once the chin rotates forward — mento-posterior: caesarean, since no mechanism exists
Mento-anterior: caesarean section in every case — mento-posterior: vaginal delivery after manual rotation
Both mento-anterior and mento-posterior: caesarean section without any trial of labour
Both mento-anterior and mento-posterior: a trial of forceps from the pelvic floor
exp: Mento-anterior can deliver vaginally once the chin is to the front; persistent mento-posterior has no mechanism of labour and needs caesarean section.

opts: Empty the bladder, give oxytocin and repeat controlled cord traction; if it fails, manual removal under short anaesthesia
Empty the bladder, give oxytocin and repeat controlled cord traction; if it fails, proceed straight to hysterectomy
Leave it with antibiotics for 24 hours and reassess the next morning before intervening
Give misoprostol into the vagina and wait for spontaneous expulsion over the next six hours
exp: A trapped placenta needs a full bladder emptied, a uterotonic and controlled cord traction, escalating to manual removal if it is still retained.

opts: Fetal distress, convulsions, and manoeuvres that need a hand inside the uterus, such as manual removal of the placenta
Elective caesarean at 39 weeks, an uncomplicated placenta previa and one previous lower segment scar
Maternal heart disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and an uncomplicated twin pregnancy
Prolonged labour, maternal request for sterilisation and a previous spinal anaesthetic
exp: General anaesthesia is needed when speed matters or when the procedure needs uterine relaxation and a hand inside the uterus.

opts: 13 cm, which is greater than any antero-posterior diameter of the inlet
11 cm, which is the same as the true conjugate of the pelvic inlet
12 cm, which is the oblique diameter measured from the sacro-iliac joint
10 cm, which is the transverse diameter of the plane of least dimension
exp: The transverse diameter of the inlet is about 13 cm; the true conjugate is 11 cm and the oblique diameter about 12 cm.

opts: Gross congenital anomalies, hyperextension of the fetal neck and an estimated fetal weight at or above 4 kg
Placenta previa, oligohydramnios and a single loop of cord around the fetal neck
Cord presentation, vasa previa and a velamentous insertion of the umbilical cord
Fetal hydrocephalus, duodenal atresia and bilateral renal agenesis
exp: Ultrasound looks for the three findings that contraindicate external cephalic version: anomalies, a stargazer neck and a heavy fetus.

opts: Cephalopelvic disproportion, an unengaged head, and a fetus with a bleeding disorder or bone demineralisation
Prolonged second stage, maternal exhaustion and an epidural already sited for pain relief
Maternal cardiac disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and one previous caesarean section
Occipito-posterior position, a loose nuchal cord and lightly stained meconium liquor
exp: Absolute contraindications reflect disproportion, an unengaged head and fetal fragility; exhaustion and a long second stage are indications, not contraindications.

opts: Prostaglandin E1, the only uterotonic available as a tablet; WHO recommends 800 microgram sublingually
Prostaglandin E2, given as an intracervical gel in a dose of 0.5 mg for cervical ripening
Prostaglandin F2 alpha, given as 250 microgram intramuscularly every fifteen minutes
An oxytocin analogue, given as a 100 microgram slow intravenous bolus after delivery
exp: Misoprostol is PGE1 in tablet form; 800 microgram sublingually is the WHO regimen for prevention where oxytocin is unavailable.

opts: Carcinoma of the cervix, dense bladder adhesions, and placenta previa with large vessels over the lower segment
Breech presentation, an uncomplicated twin pregnancy and a macrosomic fetus at term
One previous lower segment scar, pregnancy-induced hypertension and gestational diabetes
Fetal distress at term, a failed induction of labour and a request for sterilisation
exp: Classical section is chosen when the lower segment cannot be reached or entered safely, not for the usual obstetric indications.

opts: Ultrasound with Doppler: placental lakes, loss of the retroplacental clear zone and an interrupted bladder line
Magnetic resonance imaging: a snowstorm appearance filling the whole uterine cavity
Computed tomography: ring enhancement of the myometrium around the placental bed
Hysteroscopy: direct visualisation of chorionic villi inside the uterine cavity
exp: Ultrasound with Doppler is the investigation of choice; the snowstorm appearance belongs to a molar pregnancy, not to accreta.

q: Management of deep transverse arrest — android pelvis : roomy pelvis.
opts: Android pelvis: caesarean section — roomy pelvis: manual or Kielland rotation followed by instrumental delivery
Android pelvis: manual rotation then forceps — roomy pelvis: caesarean section without a trial of rotation
Both android and roomy pelvis: caesarean section in every case, since rotation is never successful
Both android and roomy pelvis: vacuum extraction as the first-line treatment in the second stage
exp: Rotation then instrumental delivery is reasonable only when the pelvis is roomy; with an android pelvis caesarean is safer.

opts: Preterm: Duhrssen incisions in the cervix at 2 and 10 o'clock — term: push the body back and deliver by caesarean
Preterm: push the body back and deliver by caesarean — term: Duhrssen incisions in the cervix at 2 and 10 o'clock
Preterm: immediate craniotomy to allow vaginal delivery — term: Zavanelli manoeuvre then caesarean section
Both preterm and term: Piper's forceps are the first and only option for the trapped head
exp: Before viability the cervix is incised to release the head; at term the body is pushed back and the baby is delivered by caesarean.

opts: Post-term pregnancy, maternal diabetes, maternal obesity and a male fetus
Maternal anaemia, cigarette smoking during pregnancy and first pregnancy
Pre-eclampsia, placental insufficiency and a female fetus
Maternal hypothyroidism, hyperemesis gravidarum and teenage pregnancy
exp: Macrosomia follows excess substrate (diabetes, obesity, postmaturity) and male sex; smoking and vascular disease cause growth restriction.

opts: Anencephaly, placental sulphatase deficiency, fetal demise and fetal Down syndrome
Maternal diabetes, polyhydramnios and an already macrosomic fetus
Cervical incompetence, placenta previa and multiple uterine fibroids
Hyperemesis gravidarum, severe maternal anaemia and Rh isoimmunisation
exp: Post-term pregnancy is linked to an absent or hypoplastic fetal pituitary-adrenal axis and to sulphatase deficiency; maternal diabetes tends to shorten gestation.

opts: Centre the cup over the flexion point, about 6 cm behind the anterior fontanelle and 3 cm in front of the posterior one
Centre the cup over the anterior fontanelle, so the head deflexes as traction is applied to the skull
Centre the cup over the posterior fontanelle, which is the flexion point for vacuum application
Centre the cup over the parietal eminence on whichever side of the head lies against the sacrum
exp: Correct placement is over the flexion point on the sagittal suture, which promotes flexion and minimises scalp trauma and cup detachment.

opts: 7.5 mg/day, compared with about 0.8 mg/day in the first trimester
1.0 mg/day, compared with about 0.8 mg/day in the first trimester
25 mg/day, compared with about 7.5 mg/day in the first trimester
0.5 mg/day, compared with about 7.5 mg/day in the first trimester
exp: Elemental iron needs rise steeply to about 7.5 mg/day in the third trimester, largely for the expanding red cell mass.

opts: Trial of labour, which succeeds in about 70 per cent, or an elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks
Trial of labour, which succeeds in about 30 per cent, or an elective repeat caesarean at 34 weeks
Elective repeat caesarean at 36 weeks only, since a trial of labour is never offered after a scar
Induction with prostaglandins at 38 weeks, followed by a trial of labour in every woman with a scar
exp: A trial of scar succeeds in roughly seven out of ten women; prostaglandins are avoided because they raise the rupture risk.

opts: Where the artery turns upwards in the broad ligament, taking a bite of myometrium and staying close to the uterus
At its origin from the internal iliac artery, before the vessel crosses the lateral pelvic wall
At the level of the cervicovaginal junction, below the point where the vessels enter the cervix
At the cornual end of the uterus, where it anastomoses with the ovarian artery near the fundus
exp: The O'Leary stitch is placed where the uterine artery turns up beside the uterus, including myometrium so the suture cannot slip and avoiding the ureter.

opts: Oxytocin with controlled cord traction, then manual removal under anaesthesia if the placenta is still retained
Oxytocin with controlled cord traction, then immediate hysterectomy if the placenta is still retained
Methotrexate to dissolve the adherent placenta, followed by surgical evacuation a week later
Conservative management with antibiotics and observation for 24 hours before any intervention
exp: When the placenta is simply adherent and not bleeding, oxytocin and controlled cord traction come first, with manual removal as the next step.

opts: Excruciating perineal pain with inability to pass urine, and a tense bluish tender swelling of the vulva
A painless soft swelling of the vulva with fever and offensive lochia after the delivery
Painless vaginal bleeding with an open cervical os in the first week after delivery
Pruritus with a watery discharge and superficial dyspareunia in the early puerperium
exp: A vulval haematoma is intensely painful, causes retention of urine and appears as a tense bluish swelling that may extend into the thigh.

opts: The after-coming head becomes trapped, causing fetal hypoxia and intracranial haemorrhage
Shoulder dystocia with brachial plexus injury from traction on the extended arms
Uterine inversion from traction on the cord during delivery of the placenta
Cord avulsion with fetal exsanguination before the trunk has been delivered
exp: The deadly complication of breech delivery is entrapment of the after-coming head, which is why the head must never be rushed.

q: Type of uterine contraction produced — oxytocin : methylergometrine.
opts: Oxytocin: physiological, with relaxation between contractions — methylergometrine: tetanic, without relaxation
Oxytocin: tetanic, without relaxation between contractions — methylergometrine: physiological, with relaxation
Both drugs produce a tetanic contraction of the uterus that does not relax at all
Both drugs produce physiological contractions with complete relaxation between them
exp: Oxytocin produces physiological contractions with relaxation, whereas ergometrine produces a sustained tetanic contraction and is unsafe before delivery.

opts: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn, operative and anaesthetic risks, and consequences for future pregnancies
Uterine rupture in labour, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and shoulder dystocia at delivery
Severe perineal trauma, pelvic floor dysfunction and anal sphincter injury after the birth
Post-term pregnancy, meconium aspiration syndrome and cord prolapse during labour
exp: Elective caesarean raises neonatal respiratory morbidity and complicates later pregnancies; it protects against perineal trauma and shoulder dystocia.

opts: Ruptured membranes, oligohydramnios, placenta previa, an abnormal cardiotocograph or a uterine scar
Pregnancy-induced hypertension, fetal growth restriction and mild iron deficiency anaemia
One previous lower segment caesarean section and well-controlled maternal heart disease
A gestation of 36 weeks, an anterior placenta and a maternal age above thirty-five years
exp: Absolute contraindications make version unsafe; a previous lower segment caesarean and 36 weeks are relative considerations, not absolute bars.

opts: Complete forward rotation, which is commonest; incomplete forward rotation; and persistent posterior rotation
Persistent posterior rotation, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and deep sacral arrest
Incomplete forward rotation, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and face-to-pubis delivery
Deep sacral arrest, which is commonest; complete forward rotation; and persistent posterior rotation
exp: Most occipito-posterior heads rotate forwards completely to occipito-anterior; the rest rotate incompletely or persist as occipito-posterior.
